utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is Tuesday, January 26th, 2010, and I greet, first and foremost, Ms. Biersay and Mr. Marcussen, and all the people helping them, Mr. Seselj, and I also greet everyone helping us in this courtroom. Let's first move into closed session. Could the usher please drop the blinds, and we will bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, please stand up, because I'm going to ask you to provide us with your first name, last name, and date of birth. Please state your name, first name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vojislav, my surname is Dabic. I was born on the 28th of July, 1966, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present, I am working as a driver, but my actual profession is electrician.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify in this Tribunal or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you testify in a domestic court in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This way, no. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. I asked you whether you had testified in this Tribunal before, you said you hadn't. So you never came to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time for me to come to this country, never mind this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I had understood initially. Let me tell you how things are going to be. You're a Chamber witness. You were called to testify by the Trial Chamber. The three Judges have divided the work between them. For 30 minutes, I'm going to have questions for you on the way you had contacts with the OTP and with Mr. Seselj's counsel or associates in order to find out how all that happened, so these are the questions I'm going to put to you. Then Judge Lattanzi and Judge Harhoff will ask questions of you in relation to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1993, events that you were a witness to. My colleagues will each take 30 minutes, so in all in all we'll have one hour and a half. Thereafter, the Prosecutor, I believe Ms. Biersay, will have one hour and a half for her question. She can submit to you all sorts of documents, any documents she wishes to show you. Then Mr. Seselj will have the same amount of time for his questions, whatever they may be. Let's not waste any time, because altogether, you see, three times 90 minutes, that's close to five hours, and we only have two days for your testimony. You've already made the solemn oath, so you are a witness of the Chamber. You're not supposed to have any contact whatsoever. So when you go back to your hotel, you can't make a phone call, you can't say anything about the questions put to you. Once it's over, you do whatever pleases you. So did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First question: Can you tell me the circumstances in which the OTP Prosecutors got in touch with you? When did they start, in which year?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The first meeting was in the year 2000. I did not contact them myself directly. This went through a certain individual who contacted a lady, Jasmina Ploskic from Mostar, who is working in Sarajevo or, rather, in Mostar. She has an office for missing persons. Five or six times, she called me and asked for me, and in the end I agreed. And we met between the town of Brcko, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Tuzla, at a market-place called Arizona, in a cafe called Partner. She came, and I assume her husband, Senad Sejno Hadziomerovic, and Mr. Luka Radovic. I arrived. We met there, we had lunch there, and we spent some three hours together. And while we were having lunch, we discussed the fact that she had contacts with certain people from the United Nations who were looking for a potential witness, a person who had spent the entire duration of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not just in one place but at several locations there. And that is how they found me. I agreed. In the meantime, as after the war I went to Novi Sad, where I did various jobs, my family from Mostar called me on several occasions to inform me that certain persons were coming to their home, threatening them, that once they threw two hand-grenades, that at the entrance of my house they hung up a deceased notice with my picture on it, so that after certainly five persistent calls by Ms. Jasmina Ploskic, that I finally one day agreed to meet with her. We met at this market in the Partner Restaurant which no longer exists there, if you need the information, and I agreed to meet with her -- I'm sorry, with Ms. Brigitte in Sarajevo, in what used to be the students hostel, now the headquarters of the United Nations, in the Nedzarici district. This was in the year 2000. I spent four days there. On the first day, they put me up in a district called Osijek which is predominantly inhabited by Croats, and a motel called Delminium. I went down for dinner, I had dinner, and 10 men in uniform came in with the insignia of the Croatian Army. I was not indifferent to this fact. And the next day, when Ms. Brigitte, with the interpreter Majda from Tuzla, came to fetch me, I asked them to move me out of this motel, and that is what they did. Then the interviews lasted from 9.00 in the morning. We had lunch in the big canteen at the UN headquarters in Nedzarici, at the hostel, and this would go on usually until 3.00 or half past 3.00. It depended. So we started with the basic things, who I am, what I'm doing, what I used to do, until we reached for what was for her the most important area; that is, my participation in the war, where, what, how, who I saw, who was there, where they were, what they were doing. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you. So you met with Ms. St. Germain on the 13th of November, and you had a talk with her - I'm not going to go into the details of it - this in 2001 [as interpreted]. I guess that they drew up a report stating everything you said then. And you were shown the document, which you signed. You signed the document. Did you sign the document on the document written in English or on the document written in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document was written in English, in the English language, just as I see now on the monitor, words in English, and you're addressing me in French.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I rise to direct your attention to page 15, line 13. It says in the year of 2001, and I think it was 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, in November 2000. Thank you. When you signed the documents, there was an interpreter next to you. Did the interpreter read back the entire text to you in your own language or just ask you to sign the document?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreter -- or let me repeat. The document was certainly in English. It was typed out on a laptop. And I noticed, while making statements -- I understand English at least to some extent, and even some French, and I think that the statement was changed. I signed only the English text. I did not receive anything in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have here another statement, dated 10th of June, 2004. Did the OTP contact you again in order to obtain another statement from you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Though this was a long time ago, I think that I was contacted by Mr. Rovija, something like that. I can't remember the surname exactly. It was a long time ago. And he read my statements that I had made to Ms. Brigitte, and he told me that most probably I would not be needed by the Tribunal or the United Nations. I answered, I don't believe so. You will look me up again. And that is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you signed the second statement. Were you at any time told that you were going to be called to testify in the Seselj case or in another case? Were you told in which proceedings you might testify or weren't you told anything at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I am able to recollect, they didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't tell you anything. Were you promised money, resettlement, relocation, or a job? Were you made any promises or threats, or was this just, let's say, a technical interview in which nothing particular happened?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting with Ms. Brigitte, she said to me and suggested that I could, for example, go to America, to work on a farm there, that I would have a good salary, that I would receive money. And the money that I did receive from Ms. Brigitte was simply my daily allowances, that is, for the days I was absent from work, and my ticket; in other words, travelling expenses that they covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I wish to know about contacts you had with Mr. Seselj's Defence. The Prosecutor has received statements -- or received statements then. You were not called to testify. What happened? Did you call them, were you called? Tell us exactly how it all happened.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sent, by mail to the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party in Zemun, a note saying that I would like to get in touch with the Defence team for Dr. Vojislav Seselj. So this was sent by mail. And I know for certain that it was received at the porters of the Serbian Radical Party in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you feel the need to tell the Serbian Radical Party that you wanted to testify? Why did you do so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, regardless of the fact that Dr. Vojislav Seselj is here present, I think, in my view, this was unjust towards him, and I decided on my own -- for days I couldn't sleep, or, rather, nights, and I decided to make this move to change my statement and not to be a witness for the Prosecution in the proceedings against Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did you meet among Mr. Seselj's associates? Who were your contacts?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I met with Mr. - if he's a gentleman, and I think he is - Jadranko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times did you meet with him; twice, five times? How many times?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Whenever I received a call from the Prosecution, I would inform him, or, rather, we informed you, too, through the Tribunal that I do not wish to be a Prosecution witness in the case against Dr. Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You made statements to Dr. Seselj's associates. Did they receive them in person, based on what you said to them? Did they then ask you to sign the documents? How did it all happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally, myself, wrote those statements, which we carried to the Court in Novi Sad for certification, and the Court in Belgrade. I remember well it was the 4th Communal Court in Belgrade, Municipality of Zemun. I, myself, and Mr. Jadranko Vukovic went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a question. For certification of your signature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: In connection with these statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was about the signature. You did not give a statement before any official Serbian authority; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: No, no. All the statements I signed, myself, by hand, and with my ID documents, both in the Court in Novi Sad and in the Court in Belgrade, or, rather, Zemun, which is part of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To authenticate your signature; was that the purpose?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, and the Court gave a stamp -- put a stamp on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your signature? The seal of the Tribunal was put on the signature, on your signature, to confirm that the signature at the end of the document is, indeed, the signature of Mr. Vojislav Dabic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Quite so, exactly so, because no document can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Dabic, when you said you wrote, yourself, the declaration that you gave to the Defence, did you write it in your handwriting and it was then later typed out, or did you type it, yourself, on a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Harhoff, I personally wrote this statement on a piece of paper from a notebook, and I really cannot type. I don't know how to type. So I wrote it out in a notebook with lines, a notebook with lines, and not with squares. So I, personally, wrote out the statement maybe while you were sleeping. At night, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who typed it out; do you know?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As I was sending this to Belgrade, Mr. Jadranko Vukovic, with the Defence team for Dr. Vojislav Seselj, they typed it out. So exactly the way I had written it, that was typed out. And I checked this, I verified it, both my statement and their typed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then I will let my fellow Judge Ms. Lattanzi ask questions and I'll be done. When you met Mr. Jadranko Vukovic, can you tell us whether he threatened you, whether he offered money, whether he told you about a possible job that you may have, or did he just tell you, You contacted us; give us your statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jadranko Vukovic did not offer me any kind of job, he did not give me any money, because I worked in Novi Sad, where I live. I worked in a small cafe, so I didn't really need money. I mean, it wasn't only him. Other people from the Defence team didn't offer me anything either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. Could you tell us whether you're a member of the Serbian Radical Party today; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I am not a member of any party, including the Radical Party, for the following reason: I'm not interested in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally my last question. You mentioned my fellow Judge by name earlier, and you also called me by name. I didn't know I was that famous. Why is it that you know my name?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I see your name right now on the monitor in front of me. Also, on the summons that I received from the Court to testify, it also says very nicely what your name is, as far as I know. I have the summons here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, absolutely, my name is on the monitor. Ms. Biersay, Ms. Lattanzi will ask questions now first.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I just had a question with respect to -- we've discussed many statements, and I thought perhaps for the record it might be helpful to refer to the 65 ter numbers that they have been assigned, just to keep track of them for the Court's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once you have the floor, you can provide us with all the numbers. I had questions -- general questions to ask. I didn't want to go into details. But maybe my fellow Judge will. I don't know. But later on, when it's your turn, you can say that the November statement has this 65 ter number. I only had 30 minutes, and I didn't want to waste my time. I give the floor to Ms. Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's one thing I would like to ask you first, something that has to do with the questions put to you by Judge Antonetti. I would like to know whether, while you were making these statements to Ms. Brigitte -- Ms. Brigitte, I can't remember her last name, I'd like to know whether an interpreter was there. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The interpreter was a lady, a young lady, either Ms. or Mrs. - I didn't ask her exactly, Majda from Tuzla, that's for sure, and I was sitting the way I'm sitting now and talking to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did this interpreter do, exactly? She didn't do anything? She did not read back the statement in Serbian, this statement that had been written in English?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you quite frankly, as I've sworn at the very outset, for instance, I would say to the lady interpreter -- I would say something, and then I think that she would somehow explain this in a different way to Ms. Brigitte. So the statement that was written in English on a laptop is what she read out to me in Serbian, I mean Serbo-Croat, whatever you wish, so I concluded on that basis that there were some changes, some minor changes, in the interpretation or translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the interpreter had changed some things, they did not really translate what you had said. Obviously, that's what you said. I have a few questions, very few of them, regarding our case. At one point in time in the November 2000 statement, you mentioned some rallies where pacifist messages were given, but there were extremists who were present with cockades, singing nationalist hymns. So could you identify these people, that they belonged to a specific group?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madame, when I was speaking to Ms. Majda, I said that these were gatherings, but she translated it as "rallies." Among these people, I did not know anyone because, well, during the war I, myself, wore a sajkaca cap and a cockade. Perhaps there were five or six of them dressed that way. Well, when a person comes to a gathering, for example, to a football game, you have to come under the influence in order to be able to root, or to use something else that's intoxicating, drugs and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's follow the same line. In the November 2000 statement, you mention armed Chetnik volunteers, armed with light automatic weapons or with grenades. Now, I would like to know whether you can identify more specifically these volunteers which you called Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madame, again I'm going back in time. I also wore a sajkaca cap and a cockade, and they called me a Chetnik. Now, where these volunteers had come from, I cannot establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but let's go back a few minutes. In one of your statements, I read that at one point in time you said that your family was against your recruitment during the war, and you were sent to Moscow. Can you confirm this? Mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct, that is quite right. As war was looming in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a war was already underway in Croatia, and I had always believed myself to be a Serb, an Orthodox Serb - I liked Orthodoxy - my parents were afraid that I might join the ranks of the Serbian Army or the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence, so they sent me to Russia. To Moscow, to be more precise, to stay with a lady who was my father's relative, and I worked as a driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm a bit sick. But I would like to know how you decided to return to Serbia and to join the war.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: When the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I lost all contact with my family, which worried me very seriously. Then on one day my relative, and she always travelled on official business - if you wish, I can give you her full name - she travelled to Italy; Milan, to be precise. I took the train, the regular train, from Moscow to Belgrade. I arrived in Belgrade, and from Belgrade I went to Titograd, Podgorica nowadays. And then from Podgorica, I went to Nevesinje. I spent a day there and went down to Mostar. I entered the city, which had been destroyed. I entered my home. I found my mother, my sister, my nephew, and my Muslim neighbours. They were near my home because they felt safe there. That is to say that I was wandering about town as a civilian. A lot of people didn't like that. Before the war and -- before the war and now, and to the end of my days, I was fond of Orthodoxy, and I joined the Territorial Defence of the town of Mostar; the eastern part of town, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What convinced you to join the TO, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, I, as a civilian, 25 years old, could not just walk around town just like that, while other people had joined in. I went to the nearby neighbourhood of Zelik, where the TO headquarters was. That's where I was issued with a uniform and rifle, a PAP rifle. I was on night duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in this same statement, November 2000, you also mention about the Chetnik members of the Karadjordje unit, and you mention a man called Arsen Grahovac. I would like to know a little bit more about this group, and I would like to know whether they had any connection with Seselj and Seselj's volunteers.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madame Judge, it is correct that in Nevesinje there was a detachment called Karadjordje. However -- well, they did call them Chetniks, but because they wore -- they wore Chetnik insignia, cockades. The late Arsen Grahovac was their leader. That was shown on television as well. However, the members of the Karadjordje Detachment were exclusively members of the Serbian Renewal Movement, the SPO, because at that time in Nevesinje and in the surrounding area, and throughout Eastern Herzegovina, there was no Serb Radical Party. The SPO, as we know full well, has as its president Mr. Vuk Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right. At that moment, there weren't any. Now, you say that the Serbs were in Nevesinje and Mostar, and there were 70 Serbs fighting there, and you say that they were helped by the JNA. However, you don't say who paid the members of this Karadjordje unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, it is correct that we received money from the JNA. There were Serbs in Mostar and Nevesinje, the Neretva River Valley, all of the Neretva River Valley, that is. You're right about. And on the 25th of May, the JNA withdrew from Mostar and from all of Eastern Herzegovina. As for money for the Karadjordje Detachment, in my view, I can just say that it is probable that they received the money from the SPO, the Serbian Renewal Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the June 2004 statement, you mention 20 or 30 of Seselj's men who would have come from Serbia two or three days after the reservists of the JNA. Their local commander was a man called Boban. Did you know about this directly or did you hear this through hearsay?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madame Judge, while I was in Mostar, before I was wounded, I heard that there was a small group of some 30 men who had come from Serbia. I had never seen them in town. We were in town, for the most part; we, the Territorial Defence. Allegedly, they were the garrison command. Allegedly, they did not go into town at all. I think that they were led by a man whose name started with a B. As I did not really walk around town very much, it was one of these walks that I hardly took that cost me a sniper bullet in my left arm. So I don't really remember that much. However, I did not see them in town. As for the garrison command, it had been relocated outside town, above town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you also told how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no one had said anything to me about how they were dressed. We, at any rate, were all dressed in olive-green-grey uniforms that had remained in the warehouses after the JNA had left, so it would be a uniform with this and that kind of insignia. I repeat to you, once again, that I wore a sajkaca cap and a cockade, I had a beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether this group, which was wearing these emblems and the cockade which were not the official insignia of the JNA nor the TO, I guess, could you tell us whether this was a group which met at the Azaro Cafe?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The Azaro Cafe was in the western part of the town of Mostar, that is to say, on Croat territory. These groups that you are referring to, they were probably reservists who had arrived just before the war broke out. They arrived in Mostar, and the owner was a Serb, and of course they went to drink there. However, I don't think that they were from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 2000 statement, you mention a check-point held by Seselj's men. Could you give us more information on this, tell us, for example, how you found this out?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also say that it was a man named Kinez who was commanding this check-point?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: When I arrived from Russia to Mostar, or, rather, on the road between Nevesinje and Mostar, there was a sort of check-point. There were five or six men in uniform. And I, indeed, had arrived with the military police from Nevesinje. It was a Renault 5 vehicle, and I asked the driver, Who are these men? And he said to me, Ah, it's some guy called Kinez. That's what they call him. Possibly he's from Serbia. So nothing happened. They stopped us, and since they saw that they were in uniform, they said, Who's this man in civilian clothes? That was I. They explained that I was a young man from Mostar and that I was going home. It wasn't that he was called "Knez." He was called "Kinez."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I'm going to return to the relationship between Mr. Seselj and the man called Grahovac, because you didn't really answer my question. So could you -- when you said that he was in charge of security with the help of Chetnik volunteers, and you're also saying in your 2004 statement that he created the Chetnik Serbian Movement and that he would have -- allegedly would have met Seselj in Belgrade, and Bozidar Vucurevic in Trebinje. I would like some details on all this, all this information that you have in your statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Near my home in Mostar, I had a friend who had originally hailed from Nevesinje, or, rather, a village nearby. He knew the late Arsen Grahovac very well. When he would come to see me, he would tell me that Arsen Grahovac allegedly went to Belgrade to see Dr. Vojislav Seselj, which I really do not believe. It is quite possible that he did meet up with Mr. Bozidar Vucurevic, the mayor of Trebinje. Trebinje is about 100 kilometres away from Nevesinje. Again, I repeat to you that the late Arsen Grahovac was a member of the SPO. Well, for some people, he was a Chetnik too. These men who were with him, or soldiers, of course, they were Chetniks for some people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this 2004 statement, you talk about Grahovac. You talk of him as if he was responsible for a lot of massacres and looting in the Nevesinje region, and you connect him with Seselj's volunteers?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madame Judge, I'm saying to you yet again that all the soldiers down there at the front-line who wore these nationalist insignia or cockades were called "Seselj's men." As for the massacre that you refer to, for which perhaps the late Arsen Grahovac is responsible, I really do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the one who said that. You did in your 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Probably because at that time the Muslim inhabitants started to be expelled, and they were active in the territory of Nevesinje municipality, because there were quite a number of Muslim villages there, and there still are. But that I had heard that some people had been slaughtered or killed, probably because the Muslims were armed too, they were not naive, so someone had to be responsible, and it is always the commander who is responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody is bound to be responsible. But in your statement, you mentioned Grahovac expressly, and you put him together with Seselj's volunteers. Therefore, now you deny what you said then? Well, even if we haven't had a whole 30 minutes, but, I mean, Judge Harhoff has some questions for you, but this is -- or this was my last question for you.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not denying that, but it is not clear to me why you persistently say and keep repeating the expression "Seselj's volunteers." That is not clear to me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are the one using those terms in your statements, not me. Please, don't make -- or don't claim that I am saying something whilst this is taken from your own statement, Witness.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I just told you that I am not denying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Judge Lattanzi has had her 30 minutes. We're going to have a break now. After the break, Judge Harhoff will ask some questions of you. We're going to stop for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dabic, I have a few questions to you relating to the statement that you have given to the Defence, and also a few questions relating to the information that you provided in the statements to the Defence and to the Prosecution. Now, first of all, Mr. Dabic, you told me, when I asked you during the first session, that you had written your statements to the Defence of Mr. Seselj in your handwriting because you do not know how to handle a typewriter. And if I understand your statement correctly, it was you who contacted the Defence organisation in Belgrade, and you did so from Novi Sad, where you lived. Is that correct, that you were in Novi Sad when you contacted the Defence in Belgrade? And where exactly did you write your statement? Did you write your statement with your handwriting at home in Novi Sad and then mailed it to Belgrade, or how was that done?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: What you just said at the beginning is quite right. I wrote my statement in my apartment in Novi Sad, Gradinarova Street, number 24, on an ordinary piece of paper with a Biro, and I mailed it to the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party in Zemun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you said also that you had checked the typewritten version and compared it to your handwritten version, and do you testify that there was full equality between the two, is that correct, that when you saw finally the typewritten version of your statement you compared it to the handwritten statement and you were satisfied that it was exactly the same? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So are we to understand that the version of the statement that you provided to the Defence -- we only have it in the typewritten version, but that is exactly similar to the written version that we have in front of us -- sorry, to the handwritten version that you sent? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Fully, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you receive any guide-lines as to how such a statement should be worded, should be formulated?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I wrote the statement to the best of my knowledge or, rather, as requested by the Defence team, and I put down what I could remember because, after all, it was a long time before that that the war was. So believe me, I can't remember what I ate three days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Nor can I, so that shouldn't worry you. No, but I'm interested in how you arrived at putting this statement together, and my question was to you if you were given any instructions as to how to put together the statement that you provided to the Defence. Any guide-lines or instructions, or did you simply just sit down by yourself and then wrote the statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I wrote the statement in the way that the Defence team asked me to, as soon as I contacted them. They didn't say that I should say anything in favour of Dr. Vojislav Seselj. I just wrote down what I could remember, what had happened on those days. And if I had known, perhaps we could have brought the statement that I wrote myself, and then you would see that that is true and that it was certified in court and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right. We're speaking about two statements, are we not, in May and June 2007? One in May and one in June 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I wrote five statements, and those are the first two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When you first contacted the Defence team in Belgrade, did you call them by phone, or did you go and see them, or how was the communication made?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: After I had written the first statement, at the end of the statement I signed my name, I put down my home address in Novi Sad, I provided a contact telephone number both at home and at work; that is, the cafe where I worked. And then they called me up. I got on a bus and I went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So was it after that you had met them in Belgrade that you wrote the statement or was it before?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, I apologise, Your Honour. I met them after sending the statement. So I first sent the statement with my address and the telephone number, and after that we met and spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, your statements, the first two of them, at least, they both have a short preamble in which you introduce yourself. If I quote from the preamble of your statement, it says: "I, Vojislav, son of," so-and-so, "born," this and that date, and then you quote your personal identity number, "hereby state:" And then your statement follows. Was that also your own formulation that you put in your handwritten statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent. Yes, I can give you the arguments to prove it. The number of my ID card, my personal identification number, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure that all the details that you have provided are correct. I was merely interested in the form, that it was your own idea to begin your statement by adding or by putting this short preamble in which you introduced yourself with all the details, and then you go on to say that you hereby state, and then follows the statement. If I can show you physically, then I'll show what I mean. Can you see this paper? This is your statement. And the first little paragraph here, was that also your own formulation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Meaning it was not added by someone else? This was also -- also would appear in your first original handwritten statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote all that down myself because -- well, this is not connected to this, but I was living alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, this was just to clarify the process of putting together your statements to the Defence, and I have exhausted that first question. My second question relates to your own indication of your not being interested in politics at all. That's what you told us in the beginning of your testimony today, that you had no interest in politics, yet you also testified that you attended the meetings wearing a sajkaca cap, and a cockade, and otherwise wearing a long beard and, you know, you made yourself look like a Chetnik, and that seems to me to be quite a strong political standpoint that you not only had but also displayed in the public. So do you consider your physical appearance to be completely non-political or apolitical, as you claimed you were?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, sir, as I was living and working in Mostar, I mostly worked as a taxi-driver, so I would transport people to these gatherings for money, and I accompanied them there. So if you drive someone there, then you have to -- you don't have to, but you're there, present, and then they see you there, and then they say, He came to the meeting, if that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you were seen at the meetings and that you looked like a Chetnik, but my question was really different. My question was that if you were serious about not entertaining any political preference and not being interested at all in political matters, then it was a surprise to me that you also said that you were wearing a sajkaca cap, and cockades, and all the -- not all, but at least some of the other physical symbols that pertain to Chetniks, such as the long beard and so on, because that's not -- to me, at least, is not non-political. That is, on the contrary, very political, that you have taken a standpoint. And I'm uninterested in which standpoint you have taken, but, on the one happened, you cannot maintain, at least in my view, that you have no interest in politics and yet, at the same time, dress up as someone belonging to a clearly politicised view. Do you see my problem? Mr. Dabic, I mean, come on. If you were honest about not having any political interest, then dressing up as a Chetnik would only make sense if you would say that, well, you know, you did only this -- you only dressed up like a Chetnik for some reason of, I don't know, acceptance or something, but that you really didn't mean to entertain the views that were held -- the political views that were held by many Chetniks. So either your statement about being unpolitical is wrong or your reasons for dressing up like a Chetnik were false. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honour Judge Harhoff, if I had continued -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina in those days, there were, indeed, many such meetings. If I had continued to attend those meetings, then I probably wouldn't be an ordinary individual. I would have probably got more deeply involved in politics. It is well known who are the real politicians, what they're doing and how they're doing it. The fact that I went there with friends, I can't say that it is absolutely disconnected to politics or propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's drop the subject and move on to something else. I have a few questions relating to the information that you provided in your statements to the Prosecution, and these pieces of information that you gave here in your statements to the Prosecution would seem to indicate that you knew somehow that Mr. Arsen Grahovac was somehow involved in several killings of non-Serb civilians. And my question to you is: How did you know that? Did he tell you so, that he had been involved in those killings?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Harhoff, first of all, Nevesinje is 45 kilometres from Mostar, and I lived in Mostar, whereas the late Arsen Grahovac was living in Nevesinje and he had his detachment Karadjordje. So these are all things that I heard. I didn't see it. Had I seen it, I would have been in his unit. But I was living in Mostar, and they were in the area of Nevesinje Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, but my question goes to the reliability of the information that you provided. You said at several occasions that you had heard that he had been involved in crimes, and my interest is to know just how did you learn this. Did he, himself, tell you so? You came to know him later on, and so did he at any occasion tell you directly that he was a member of the SRS and that he had been involved in those killings, and other crimes, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: First of all, the late Grahovac was not a member of the Serbian Radical Party at all. He was a member of the Serbian Renewal Movement, and these are two different concepts. The Serbian Renewal Movement is the party of Mr. Vuk Draskovic. And I met the late Grahovac once in Nevesinje. He had his own cafe there called Ravno Gora, and his soldiers would come there in a drunken condition, and they would say all kinds of things. And these were not large premises, so you could hear them talk. Here we're back from, for instance, a village, Kljuna, in Nevesinje Municipality, inhabited by Muslims. We've expelled them, this and that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when you heard these things in his cafe, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: This was roughly in the summer. I'll tell you in a minute. I was wounded in June, so about October, when the non-Serb population started to be expelled, because after I was wounded on the 13th of June, I wasn't there for two months. I was in a military hospital in Meljine near Herceg Novi, I think I told you that, and that's where the wounded would go to be treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So I'm just trying to get an idea of when you heard that the late Mr. Grahovac had been involved in some killings. Was that in the spring or was it in the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in the spring, to the best of my knowledge, if I remember well, because had it been in the autumn of 1992, I came there in June and the autumn comes after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It certainly does. But you heard it before you were wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So at some point before the 13th of June, 1992, you heard in his cafe that the late Mr. Grahovac had been involved in some sort of killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. Yes, that is so, but I can't tell you now that I saw him kill 10 or 15 men. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you perfectly well. And we're not talking about you having seen or witnessed any such crime. We are exclusively dealing with the information that you provided to the Prosecution, in which you say that you heard that the late Mr. Grahovac had been involved in some killings. And you heard this, we now understand, at some point before the 13th of June, 1992. Very well.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: That is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And let me try and get a little closer to that information. Did you hear him, Mr. Grahovac, himself, or the late Mr. Grahovac, I should say? Did you hear himself say these words or was it just something that was said in the cafe when you heard it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I heard this in the cafe. And had I been a member of his unit, then I would be able to confirm 100 per cent that that is so. You understand? I just heard this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But who did you hear it from? Who said it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I heard it from his soldiers in the cafe, the soldiers who were there in a half-drunken state. They were talking, and I didn't stay there long because most of them were all drunk and armed, because during the war these killings would happen in the cafes when the soldiers would come back from the front drunk and then a rifle or a pistol would just go off on its own accord. And I apologise. Let me just add, you know that a cafe is a good source of information. You can hear everything in a cafe. That's why they should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe. Was Mr. Grahovac, himself, present when you heard it in the cafe, that day when you heard this talk about the killings?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So he was there physically present, himself. Did he confirm? Did he say, Yes, yes, we did that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So the information that you provided to the Prosecution was that you heard from Mr. Grahovac, himself, that he and/or his soldiers had been involved in several incidents of killings, and you heard so before the 13th of June, 1992? Is this correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I just told you a moment ago that his bar or cafe, it wasn't very big, so the conversation could be heard loud and clear. And when a man is drunk, believe me, he always tells the truth. And, furthermore, it wasn't just he who was saying this. It was his fighters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is a saying that you shall always be able to hear the truth from children and drunken men, so maybe this was -- Mr. Dabic, let me just go back to what we discussed a little while ago about the political party membership of Mr. Grahovac, or the late Mr. Grahovac, because you told us that he had been a member of Mr. Draskovic's party. But in your statements of May 2007, I think it was -- sorry, in your statement to the Prosecution from June 2004, you seem to be saying that Mr. Grahovac was actually a member of the SRS in Nevesinje, so my question is: Did Mr. Grahovac at any later point become a member of the SRS in Nevesinje or is what you told the Prosecution just misunderstood here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I told you nicely. I could say a billion per cent that the late Grahovac was a member of the Serbian Renewal Movement. Now, I don't know how this was interpreted, because that is correct. 99 per cent of the SPO, the Serbian Renewal Movement, and I must repeat again that quite certainly, neither before nor during the war, was there a Serbian Radical Party in Nevesinje, nor was there any initiative to form such a party, and regardless of the fact that Mr. Vojislav Seselj is present here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand, but I just wanted to clarify the information here. So I understand that this is a possible mistake that sneaked itself into the statements taken by the Prosecution. Let me move on to a related issue in that same statement from June 2004, because on the next page of that statement you seem to be saying the following, and I'm now quoting from your statement. This is what you have said to the Prosecution. You were referring to Mr. Grahovac, and you say the following: "His group was responsible for killings and cleansing of places like the 1st Ladjice Kula close to Gacko, Buna, Mostar, Bijelo Polje, and also in Pijesci, which was on the way to Stolac from Mostar. They committed the worst crimes in Nevesinje in the village of Sopilja, where they killed more than 100 people." This, I understand, relates to what you may have heard or what you heard in the cafe. And then you go on to say: "In Mostar, there was another Chetnik unit. There were about 50 of them in that unit. They were wearing Chetnik insignias, the cocarde and the two-headed eagles, and we all knew they were Seselj's volunteers from Serbia. The unit did not have a particular name." Now, my Dabic, I'm interested in knowing how you learned that this other group of volunteers, about 50 of them, were Seselj's volunteers. Please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I keep parroting the same thing time and again. The group was at the command of the garrison in town. They did not enter town at all, but I did hear -- I didn't see anyone, though, and I didn't dare go up there because of sniper activity throughout town, so I could not establish exactly that it was Seselj's men, Chetniks, as it were. However, I heard from other people that they were certainly from Serbia, that they spoke like Serbians from Serbia. Now, how they came, in which way, who had sent them, well, most of them came as volunteers, voluntarily. Do you understand what I'm saying? I mean that, say, wherever there's shooting, We go there. Most of them must have come without anyone's knowledge, just as what you said a few moments ago about Arsen's group. This was practically a wandering unit. They board a bus and they go. Just before the war, on the Mostar-Nevesinje road, they put up barricades just on their own. They stopped cars. The police didn't dare do anything about it, so they did whatever they wanted to do and they went wherever they wanted to go. But it is certainly proven with good arguments that this group of Seselj's volunteers or Seselj's men -- I don't know how they got down there, but they certainly did not walk around the town of Mostar. At least I did not see them. Many of the things that happened was ascribed to them. They were not there on their own, though. The Territorial Defence was there, too. I was a member of the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, and let's just clarify this. You were a member of the TO because you joined the TO. And you say that various groups of Chetniks were there as well, but that they acted very independently. You just told us that they did whatever they wanted to do and they went wherever they wanted to go. So how was the co-ordination taken care of between the TO and these groups?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I can remember, there was practically no co-ordination. As a matter of fact, they tried to kill a man, our Territorial Defence commander. Quite simply, they went to headquarters there and -- well, there's this other example. This group of mine of Territorials, we guarded a bridge in Mostar. It was called Zrinski Most, and it was close to my home. And these other paramilitary formations, as they're called -- well, the Neretva Valley was very big, and you'd have these unruly armed mobs, if I can call them that, that were introducing themselves as Seselj's men, as Black Wolves, White Swans, whatever. But the most important thing for them was to say that they were Seselj's men, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And were they not under any superior control, like control of by the JNA or by the municipal authorities? Did no one control them? Were they under the command of any superior authority?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I know, no. And I waged war for four years. That is to say, I went through all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in a million small places I came across these paramilitary formations. Actually, no one dared put up any resistance. Quite simply, they would take up a position, a location, and they would be there. In Mostar, for instance, there were some clashes between us and them; that is to say, the TO and paramilitary formations. That I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I now understand. But if you are in a combat operation, the crucial thing is to have full command over all the soldiers that participate in that operation, and so it would seem to be disturbing to have semi-autonomous or independent groups roaming around, doing their own thing, in the middle of a military operation. So I'm just curious to know how this actually played out in practice. You seem to be saying that, yes, there was from time to time military operations conducted. I suppose -- you have not testified, but I suppose that this would be done under the leadership of the JNA or some superior military authority. And then you would also have various paramilitary groups who were taking part, perhaps, in that operation, but not being under the command of the superior military authority. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army could not have done anything about them, I believe. Do you understand what I'm saying? An attack against a village would start, or a cleansing operation of town, say I took part in the cleansing operation of Mostar, and it was known full well who went first, these paramilitary formations. Of course, that involved looting and all the rest. The military command was really powerless. Military commanders of the JNA -- certain military commanders of the JNA were truly incapable of controlling their own army, the regular army, the JNA, let alone -- well, things were different as far as we were concerned. We had a commander, and, okay, there were quite a few bridges in Mostar. There was a group that guarded a bridge, another group that guarded the railway station, and even the gasoline stations so that people would not steal gasoline, and also the airport was guarded, the post office, other important facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: These groups that you mentioned, the group guarding the bridge, the group guarding the gasoline station, were they paramilitary groups or were they your groups, so to say, TOs?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Sir, I told you very nicely that I was a TO. That is short for "Territorial Defence." So that is what we were guarding. As we were guarding that, I don't know, nothing dangerous, if I dare put it that way, or unusual happened. For example, until the withdrawal of -- the withdrawal from the town of Mostar that had three barracks, the JNA did not go out at all, if that's what you're interested. And you told me a few moments ago that you were interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, I have exceeded my 30 minutes, so I'm going to stop now. But my interest was merely to get an idea from you, because, remember, we were not present in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, so all the information comes from you. And I was interested if you could tell us who were controlling the paramilitary groups, and your answer, if I understood it correctly, was that no one could or would control them, not even during combat operations. If this is a correct version of your testimony, then that would be my last question. But can you confirm or deny?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I'll confirm that for you. According to my assessment, it was actually an armed mob. Do you understand what I'm saying? And if there was some kind of movement, they would be the ones who went first for looting and stealing property and -- I mean, I really doubt that we had any co-ordination with them. I mean, even military commanders, one of the Yugoslav People's Army, was still down there. They were not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, in the Neretva River Valley and the Serb villages where the local population lived, those who had been armed, they did co-ordinate with our commanders, that is to say, the Territorial Defence, when the JNA left the Neretva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have a procedural question. Ms. Biersay, in a very recent written motion, dated January 25th, 2010, you asked the Trial Chamber to grant you leave to add a video-clip dealing with the Nevesinje events which occurred in 1991. In this video, there is mention of Arsen Grahovac. Could you tell me how long you've had this video?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. We did a search for the video in 2007, towards the end, or the beginning of 2008, and we couldn't find the video. The video, I believe, was located at the end of 2009, I believe. I'd have to check the records to be sure. Having checked our missing information, it didn't have a specific date, but as -- I can tell the Court that we made a request and a search in 2007, at the end, at the beginning of 2008, when the trial first commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, are you in favour or against adding this video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to say something to you. I think that yesterday, or was it the day before yesterday -- or yesterday I received that video with the latest piece of information stating that the Prosecutor might use that during their examination. I have no place to view that video. I don't have any technical equipment in my cell to view that kind of video material. However, to tell you quite frankly, I would be interested in seeing that video, and that's why I'm not opposed to it. But bear in mind the fact that the OTP did not meet their obligation vis-à-vis disclosure in a timely fashion, and I think that, therefore, they should be -- measures should be taken vis-à-vis them. But out of curiosity, I'd really like to see this, because I've never seen that man in all my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj. The Trial Chamber deliberated on this and decided to add on the 65 ter list this video, to add this video, noting that according to the statement made by Ms. Biersay, the OTP just recently unearthed this video, which might explain the late disclosure. Thank you. This being said, the list has been amended, the video has been added to it, and you may use it. Ms. Biersay, well, first we're going to ask our Registrar to provide us with a number for this video, an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that you denied my request, in view of the fact that this was not disclosed to me on time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Ms. Biersay's request is accepted. She may use the video, but we need an IC number for it. Mr. Registrar, please, could I have a number for the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The video will be Exhibit P879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, let me remind you that you have at that hour and 30 minutes. You probably won't finish tonight. We will continue tomorrow with Mr. Seselj's questions. But be very careful and look very closely -- check the time very closely. Judges abided by the time that was allotted to them -- that they had allotted, themselves, actually. So, please, we would like everyone to be just as vigilant. You have one hour and 30 minutes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And before I start my time running, I'd like to tend to some administrative issues in giving the 65 ter numbers for the statements just so that we can have a clear record, because I will be asking that some of these statements be shown to the witness. The ICTY statement that's dated 13th November, 2000, is 65 ter 7517. The ICTY statement from Mr. Dabic dated June 10, 2004, is 65 ter 7518.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Perhaps it's a question of poor interpretation. However, the interpretation I heard was that the statement was given to this Tribunal. As far as I know, this Tribunal did not take any statements. When one says "Tribunal," it means the three of you Judges. I assume that this is a statement taken by the OTP. I had other objections to the poor-quality interpretation, but this is something I simply could not remain silent about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, the statements of November 13, 2000, and June 2004 are the statements that were handed over to the OTP, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic was, indeed, interviewed by OTP investigators, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. These two statements were used by the Judges in their questions. You want to show them to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I will be showing them -- I will seek to show them, Your Honour, that's correct. The May 11, 2007, statement that was given to the Defence, and I'll call it "the Defence statement," and that was referred to by the Judges, that is 65 ter 7519. The one from June 7th, 2007, a second Defence statement -- I'm sorry, the transcript reads "65 ter 7518." The 2007 statement, the first one, is 7519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the second?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the second one is 65 ter 7520. And I believe that the Trial Chamber has another statement -- Defence statement dated August 14th, 2008, and that is 65 ter 7523.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, very well. In order for things to be very clear, please tell us -- please talk about Prosecution statements, with their dates, and Defence statements --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In summary, yes, because we're a bit confused now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate that. 65 ter number 7517 is dated November 13th, 2000. It is a statement, in common parlance, given to the OTP. 65 ter number 7518 is dated June 10th, 2004. That, too, is this witness's statement to the OTP. 65 ter number 7519 is a May 11th, 2007, statement given to the Defence by this witness. 65 ter number 7520 is dated June 7th, 2007. It's a Defence statement by this witness. 65 ter number 7523 is dated August 14th, 2008, and that, too, is a Defence statement. And for the record, in the August 14th statement Mr. Dabic lists six statements, the August 14th one being the seventh. I recognise that the Court had asked him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want to have a provisional number for all this? We'll decide on the admission later on. Could we have an MFI number for the moment, please, for all these statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 7517 will be Exhibit P880, marked for identification. 65 ter number 7518 will be Exhibit P881, marked for identification. 65 ter number 7519 will be Exhibit P882, marked for identification. 65 ter number 7520 will be P883, marked for identification. And 65 ter number 7523 will be P784 [sic], marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake on line 25. 65 ter 7523 should be MFI number P884.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, P884, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dabic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We haven't met, so I'd like to introduce myself. My name is Lisa Biersay, and I'm a trial attorney, as you may have guessed, with the Office of the Prosecutor. Is it correct that we haven't met before today?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can -- well, actually, first of all, when I talk to you, should I look at you or can I look at --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You're here for the Trial Chamber. If it makes you comfortable to make eye contact, I understand, that's fine, but your evidence is for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are talking to the Bench, but you can also watch Ms. Biersay, just like you can watch Mr. Seselj also when he will be putting questions to you, because courtesy requires for people to look at the people talking to them. And I'm sure that you're a very courteous man, so you can look at Ms. Biersay. You should look at Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right. I mean, it is proper to ask, isn't it? I mean, yes, this is the first time I see you, really, and, I mean, that's for sure. It's the first time I see you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would like to go specifically to the year 1994. I will go back to events that happened before 1994, but that's where I'd like to start is 1994. Now, in 1994, you participated in the relocation of some bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what "relocation" means. Does that mean digging up or something?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you know of a place called the Breza Pit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And perhaps at this point it would be helpful if we could see on the screen MFI P880, and if we could go to -- it would be page 37 in the English version, and I believe it would be pages 34 to 35 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So in 1994, did you participate in activities at that pit I just named, the Breza Pit, in -- near -- in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand what activities you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you there --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I mean, you mean digging up --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, were you there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I was there with a group of three more fellow combatants who took part in digging up these corpses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how is it that you knew to go there to dig up these corpses?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, an order had come from the command of the brigade that we were supposed to go there and have these bodies removed. I was at the command post of my battalion, and on that day there weren't enough men there. Four of us took a truck and went there. It was summertime. The pit was 30 metres deep, and it was 30-by-30 metres, roughly. We went down using, well, not only ropes but, I mean, whatever you call that mix of ropes and ladders. And then we started digging out rocks, because there were lots of them there, and then -- I mean, there were two of us down there in the pit and two were up there, and we were getting these bodies out. I mean, I don't know. As far as I know, we cleared everything. In our estimate, there were 42 men there. The stench was unbearable, begging your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. Now, could you describe, before we -- I want you to describe that experience to the Trial Chamber, but first could you -- you know, you talked about getting this order. Could you describe exactly what military component you were part of and to whom you reported when you received those orders?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I was in the 5th Battalion of the so-called Nevesinje Brigade, or the 8th Motorised Brigade, and that day the deputy commander of the brigade came and said that since these bodies were known about -- and I learnt about those bodies only when I arrived in the summer of 1992, maybe the 15th or 16th of June, so I learnt about the bodies. When I came back from treatment, I didn't know about the pit, nor where it was, until that day when we went there. So the commander -- the deputy commander came with a driver, and in my battalion I was an officer, an operative, so I had to attend any such events. And after talking to the deputy commander, myself and three other soldiers and with a truck, we went there with the necessary equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. But before you get to the point where after you get in the truck, what is the name of the commander who gave you the information about where you were supposed to go and what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Take your time. In the meantime, if the Registry could go to page 32 in the English, and I believe it will be page 30 in the B/C/S. Mr. Dabic, do you recall the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I think it was Novica Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was -- excuse me. And who -- it was Nikola Guzina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Nikola Guzina was my commander, the commander of the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So when you say "Novica Gusic," where does he fit in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 8th Motorised Brigade. He was a commander to my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you said you and - correct me if I'm wrong - three of your fellow -- your colleagues went in a truck to this pit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And before you left in the truck, were you told that there would be bodies in this pit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: If we were going there, we had to know why we were going there, and I told you that it was only two months later, maybe in September or August, I learnt about this particular pit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did you learn about this particular pit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I learned that a group of men had been executed there of non-Serb ethnicity who had been arrested in a mountain pass on Mount Velez, known as Teleca Lastva, and that they were brought there to the village school, that they were held there, and then they were driven over there and executed. I'm really sorry that I don't have the documents for you to see how much time I had spent in hospital so that I wasn't present there, I only heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did you do once you -- you cleared the rocks. You described that for the Trial Chamber. What did you do after that with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After clearing the pit and pulling out the bodies, we pulled them out one by one and loaded them onto the truck, and then we drove them to the foot of Mount Velez, to a location there, but myself and two soldiers. The fourth one wasn't with us. And deep within the mountain it was very difficult to find this spot. There was just the three of us who knew where this was. As there was timber-cutting nearby and there was a big log, you know, the trunk of a tree that was there, so we dug it up, and this left a big hole. We enlarged it, and so we dug the bodies into that hole and covered them with earth and stones. I think we put a dry pine tree there, too. And after that, we returned to the command post. But who didn't know where this was? It was very difficult to find this spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if I may, what kind of personal items did you see in the pit while you were removing these 42 bodies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Regarding personal items that I saw, there was a watch, there was a wooden prosthesis of a leg, and I remember well that I found among those things the bodies were already decomposing and there was something like a receipt -- like an ID card of a man who used to work in Nevesinje in a company in charge of the cleaning of the town. And I think the name and surname was Mujo Alibegovic. I'm not quite certain, but I think that was it. I also saw some running shoes, a large size, and so on. So I beg your pardon for saying it, but the stench was unbearable, but we were wearing masks. Ordinary face masks, not gas masks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you take -- you and the colleagues you mentioned, where did you take these 42 bodies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I think I just told you clearly. We drove them deep within the foot of a mountain. We went by truck as far as we could to the foot of Mount Velez, on the northern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did you take them there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: We took them there because in the brigade command they had received information that there were UN members who were already present in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they were due to come, and that they had heard from non-Serb inhabitants of Mostar that in this pit there were non-Serbs killed. So we had to remove them so that when they came, they would see that there was nothing in the pit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that it took you some years to pass that information along to someone else?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you repeat that question, please? Did I have the strength to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No. Did you, some years later, tell someone about the relocation of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And based on the information you provided, were these bodies exhumed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. In 1999, I am certain 99 per cent that they were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is it after this exhumation that you gave your first statement to the OTP in 2000?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: When I met with Ms. Brigitte, I think so, yes. I am certain that I gave that information to her. I think it was that year, but I'm quite sure that I did pass on the information, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquiry as to how much time I have, just so I can know whether I should stop now or go to another subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm just not sure how much time we have to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, you have another 15 minutes before the break. We'll break at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
