utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask you a follow-up question. As we understand, the 42 bodies -- well, the 42 people had been executed. Were they civilians or military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as what I heard, I think that there were even armed members of the Muslim army. There were soldiers, too, because weapons were found on them, apart from civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who executed them? Were they executed by your battalion or your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I can't claim and say that -- who did it. I really don't know. But this was probably during the withdrawal, when they were withdrawing from the Neretva River Valley. Now, who actually did it, I really don't know, and I don't believe -- though I said I didn't know, I don't believe that any of the paramilitary formations had done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When your unit commander told you to go and relocate the bodies, when he told you to do that, was he doing so in order to hide the existence of the pit from the international representatives who were present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did they mean to conceal? Did they want to conceal their own responsibility or did they want to hide the fact that this sort of abuse had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time that this happened, when Ms. Bier [as interpreted] mentioned this, the battalion commander was not Nikola Gusic. I really don't know when this was done. But when we went to dig them up and remove them, he was the commander. But when this was done, he was certainly not the battalion commander. Now, who was, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical detail. You were a member of a battalion. Was it a JNA battalion or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because the Yugoslav People's Army had left the Neretva Valley. When I say "the Neretva Valley," this was an area of some 50 kilometres in length. And what remained was the Territorial Defence. So the JNA was not present there at all, because this happened after their departure. It has been proven that they withdrew from the former Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 25th of May, and this happened later. So 100 per cent they weren't there, that's for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the JNA wasn't present there. And this happened after the 25th of May of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. Wasn't it the VRS that was present then as an army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Republika Srpska, as far as I can remember, it was formed after that, I think. There was just the Territorial Defence there, to the best of my knowledge, as far as I can recollect, because when I arrived, after spending two months in hospital, then it was formed as the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS. But the JNA certainly wasn't there. Now, don't think that I'm trying to defend them. I've come here to tell the truth, and to the best of my knowledge I am saying what I know, and I have sworn to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Very well. So as I understand it, it is thanks to you that the bodies were recovered, because you provided the information to the OTP investigator. And later, in 1999, the bodies were found, thanks to you, and you gave a statement one year later. Is that the chronology? You don't seem to be in agreement with this, so tell me about it. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could -- I'm sorry, the translation said, "Tell me about it, Ms. Biersay."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. "Ms. Biersay" was added by the interpreter, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please, Witness, was it through you that the bodies were discovered in 1999 because you were the one who told about them to the OTP investigator, because if you'd never said anything, the bodies would never have been recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you now. It is quite certain that I told the investigator, Ms. Brigitte. However, the exact position where the bodies were, I didn't take them there, someone else took them there, because before that I had taken this man there and shown him the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you say that to relieve your conscience or to ease your conscience or for the truth to be established, or was it in order to serve international justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to demonstrate the truth, because the relatives of those people were normally keen to find those bodies. And at the time the corpses were discovered and dug up from this second secret location, I was already in Novi Sad. So I told you a moment ago, and you probably haven't forgotten, that another man took them to this spot. This is known, even in the police archives, the Serbian police archives, and in the United Nations, that I wasn't the one who was present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Biersay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the Court, if I may direct your attention to page 34, the second paragraph from the bottom addresses the Court's question as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could pick up on the issue of the military structure at the beginning -- at the end of 1991 to, let's say, May of 1992, what -- could you describe that for the Trial Chamber? Are you familiar with the 4th Military District?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I hear of this for the first time. The 4th Military District?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How about the 13th Corps, JNA 13th Corps?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the 10th Military -- excuse me, Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: 10th Motorised? I cannot say with certainty, but I think that this was a light brigade that was in the northern part of the municipality of Nevesinje. I think that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what about the 13th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The 13th Motorised? I think -- when I say "I think," I don't want to engage in any guess-work. I think it was from Gacko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. I draw your attention, Your Honour, that this is like a quiz. We have no basis in the documents for the names of these units, so Ms. Biersay should provide some foundation. I am surprised, and not just the witness. These are names of units that I never heard of them. If she could give us any documents, any reference, because it's not in the documents for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If the Court would like me to provide something, I would be happy to after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, let's have the break, anyway, because it's now 20 to 6.00. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Biersay, where do you find all these figures about these brigades?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can hand it to you now, what is marked -- the English is marked ET04105818-04185818, and we'd ask that it be admitted or somehow kept track of. The document, as the Court will see, is entitled "Herzegovina Corps Command," strictly confidential number 147-236, and it's dated June 20th, 1992. On the back, it's signed by Commander Colonel Radovan Gurbac, I believe is how it's pronounced. That's G-u-r-b-a-c, for the Court's information. And if I could direct the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this exhibit on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, it was not, Your Honour. We moved for the admission of it based on the Court's question. My concern was that, if -- we do not see Mr. Dabic as a military expert, of course, and we wouldn't expect him to know these things, but it's to know the limits of his information, and that was the purpose for the question. He said he didn't know, and for us that's the end of it. What we would move for the admission of -- of this -- and you'll see in paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay mentioned the 4th Military District. There's no mention of that 4th Military District in this document. There's mention of the 13th and 10th Motorised Brigade, and where is the 4th Military District?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would direct the Court to the extensive testimony and report by Reynaud Theunens, who testified at the very beginning of this trial, and I believe that's discussed within his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an MFI number, and we'll see later. Registrar, could we please have an MFI number for this document dated June 20th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That will be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Madam Biersay may say that Mr. Theunens spoke about the Napoleonic Wars. She's referring us to a report of 600 or 700 pages, and when this is linked up with fragments from other cases, it could exceed 1.000 pages. I don't think this is serious. Now, why am I saying this? I will reveal a small secret, and then I'll stop. Bosnia and Herzegovina was the area of the 6th Military District of the former JNA. It included the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina and almost the whole of Slavonia. And maybe Madam Biersay made a mistake and misread the Roman numeral VI to Roman numeral IV. So I think this is not proper preparation for a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have an MFI number for this document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P885, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Biersay, as far as military districts are concerned, according to Mr. Seselj, Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of the 6th Military District and not the 4th Military District.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Again, I would refer the Court to the portion of Mr. Theunens report that discusses the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page, what page?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may get back to the Court. Specifically, I'm thinking about in his report he refers to 65 ter number 1296. And if the Court will give me a moment, I can find for you the specific references in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please continue, then, and we'll see that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could now please see -- again in MFI 880, if we could go to page 27, please. And again for the record, I'm asking for the 2000 statement that was given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Dabic, I'd like to ask you about some names that you may know. Have you heard of an individual by the name of Zdravko Kandic? And forgive my pronunciation if that's incorrect, but do you know Zdravko Kandic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what position did he hold back in 1992, specifically around June 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: In 1992, he was an operative in the brigade command, but he spent very little time in the 5th Battalion because he had a high rank. And he had had this rank before the war as an officer in reserve of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, do you know someone by the name of Dragan Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: He was the deputy of my commander; that is, Nikola Guzina's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did there come a time that he told about the massacre at Teleca Lastva?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I have already stated that I learned about those events in connection with Teleca Lastva and the Breza Pit when I came to the 5th Battalion, which is 35 kilometres to the north of Nevesinje in the direction of Sarajevo. And we spoke about that, too. These things were discussed, who was where, who had been where until then, at which front-line, and what everyone had been doing. It wasn't just he who was talking. Some other people who were there present were talking. The massacre wasn't at Teleca Lastva. That is just where the arrest took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And based on your information, where did that massacre happen?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard and learnt, the massacre occurred just above the Breza Pit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you received this information, did you also receive information about some members of the police who were involved in that massacre?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: From what I heard, not just from him but from other stories -- when I came back from hospital, I went to the 5th Battalion, or, rather, I was sent to the 5th Battalion, and I heard that certain members of the reserve police force, not active duty but reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you know -- do you know whether or not the reserve police force reported to someone above them?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: This reserve police force, maybe some 20 or so men who were up there in the 5th Battalion and who were billeted in the elementary school, they would report to the commander of the 5th Battalion, and then after a certain period of time they left the 5th Battalion and they went to those schools -- area schools, I don't know, schools that trained real policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say "5th Battalion," what do you mean? 5th Battalion of what?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion, which is part of the 8th Motorised Brigade, which had five battalions, and we were the fifth, which was the most northernmost, and it was part of the 8th Motorised Brigade. It had about one and a half thousand soldiers, which is a small number for a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, what -- could you describe to the Trial Chamber what you learned about the group of people who had been, as you described, arrested and then you heard that they were later killed? Who were in -- who was in this group?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: You mean who was captured?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, and killed, based on the information that you received.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: There may have been about 10 or so armed Muslim soldiers, and the rest were civilians. And after they were arrested, they were taken to a nearby location called Zijemlja, where there was an elementary school, and they were put in the classrooms there. And that is where they were guarded as captives. Of course, they were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you described it as a group of about 70 people. Is it true that based on the information you received, that there were women in that group?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: The information is correct that there were 70 people. There were women, yes. And if they were taken from the school, I don't know, nor did I hear whether another 30 were taken to Nevesinje or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there children in that group, based on what you heard?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there elderly in that group?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you just described that there were, I think you said -- forgive me if I'm misstating it, seven armed Muslims in that group. In your statement, you said that they were searched and that Serbs found two personal pistols. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the basis for you saying that there were seven armed people in that group, based on what you heard, of course?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you asked me a moment ago how I found out about the Teleca Lastva, and I told you that I heard it from stories recounted in the 5th Battalion. There was Djurdjic and some other people there talking, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you hear about who interrogated the men in the group that you just described?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And if we could see page 25 in the B/C/S of the exhibit that we're looking at. And it is the sentence that starts: "The men were separated ..." If we could highlight that for the witness. It should be about the fourth paragraph down, I believe. I think it's the next page -- yes, the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think it begins "Zene i --" I believe it's there. Does that read that the men were separated from the women? If you could highlight it, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: "The men were separated from the women. The men were interrogated by Kandic and Djurdjic and were only slightly beaten at this stage ..." Does that refresh your recollection about what you heard about who interrogated the men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to MFI P881. If we could go to paragraph 22 of that statement in the B/C/S and in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in describing the group of 70 civilian men in this statement, you named some people who were responsible for the killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: About the Breza Pit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At the very end of that paragraph, you describe the paragraph that we just read, you say: "A group of about 70 civilian men, women, elderly, children were captured. I want to add," and you add, "the same people are responsible for these killings." And in parentheses, it's "Red Berets" and "Seseljevci." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, you see, the Red Berets were located at Lake Borac and they came from up there, so, you see, I'm telling you only what I heard. And I tell you again, and I repeat, that there were quite a number of people down there wearing sajkacas and cockades, and they were referred to as Seseljevci, but I don't really believe that they were real Seseljevci or Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to paragraph 24, you describe a massacre happening in the upper field of Nevesinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what massacre is that that you're talking about where 200 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: This was also at the foot of Mount Velez, near the pit called "Sopilska Jama [phoen]." These were men who had come from those upper Muslim villages who were withdrawing across Mount Velez towards Mostar. They didn't succeed. They were surrounded there, and I heard that they were killed near that pit, the Sopilska Pit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you describe the people who you heard were responsible for this massacre. Did that include Colonel Novica Gusic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, they were surrounded from three sides. It says here who was in command and which commanders were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is what it says correct in your statement of 2004?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so you also named in the statement Commander Boro Antelj, correct, as participating in the massacre?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander. He had to lead someone. You can't go into battle without a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You listed Captain Zdravko Kandic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard, that he was there as well. That is to say that I mentioned the names about all of those about whom I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand. Baca Milosevic, you also heard his name connected with that massacre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was commander of those Red Berets, but it wasn't the classical Red Berets. They just called themselves that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who were they? You say they weren't classical Red Berets. Well, which Red Berets do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I heard and as far as I know, the real Red Berets were members of the police in Belgrade. They wore red berets and say the military police wore red berets. Now, everyone wanted --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I could just ask you, Arsen Grahovac, you also listed him being involved in that massacre as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, he led his own group. That is to say that he was there. That is to say that this was a well-prepared action, organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And so you describe this as a joint military operation by these five different groups led by these five different men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you say that there was a joint military operation. When did that happen? Could you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really do not remember the date, but it's possible that it was in the month of June, because again I'm telling you -- I mean, I keep saying this. I heard about all of that. I did not see that. I was not present, because at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] June of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now ask the Registrar's help in going to MFI P880 again. And this time the English page would be 24, and I think the B/C/S is 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You just described, I believe, the five battalions -- that you were part of the 5th Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, not five battalions, but the 5th Battalion. The brigade did have five battalions. You're right about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. I'm looking at what you're saying about the five battalions, and then because this was mentioned before, there was a small group of paramilitaries, some 150 men strong, led by Vuk Draskovic. Now, as to this Vuk Draskovic, was it the one who was the foreign affairs minister in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would suggest to you not to give up on that so easily. It is impossible that there were --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Seselj is more than able to bring this up in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, it's just that I was asking about Vuk Draskovic. I have some questions about it, because I know that there was a Vuk Draskovic who was the foreign affairs minister of his country, and there is another one bearing the same name who went to France, through Madame Mitterrand, so I'm asking myself is it one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know; fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that obviously the witness does not know who all the people who were foreign minister were, because these posts went by unnoticed very often. However, a position here is the one as party leader, so it's quite obvious who it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may have an opportunity to revisit the issue later on. Please continue, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe in your statement the Nevesinje Brigade, and you say that it wasn't fair for it to be called the Nevesinje Brigade because there were only around 1500 Serbs from Nevesinje; is that correct? Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what, the Nevesinje Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it a true statement or -- before I ask the follow-up question, is that true or not true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So it is true? Is that a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, but may I --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just one minute. Now, you describe how some people -- some men stayed on in Nevesinje and then others went into other areas, like Trebinje and Boracko Lake; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, can I go back a bit now? Would you allow me to do that? So --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll have you follow up. I just want you to address that point before we go back to that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And you also mention that around this time, there are about 150 men in the paramilitary group formed by the SPO, the Vuk Draskovic that we were just talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Actually, they came on two buses from Serbia. Vuk Draskovic sent them personally. I know I heard about that, and they went to the 2nd Light Brigade. That was at Lake Borac.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And now you also describe, separately from this SPO party paramilitary group of 150, that there were about 100 of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Madam, I told you very nicely that if you think that these were real Seseljevci, as it were, these were actually people from the local villages who were dressed like that, of course, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment. I'm not asking -- I understand your position. What I'm asking is: Here in your statement, you describe in one paragraph the paramilitary group belonging to the SPO, and in another paragraph you describe 100 of Seselj's men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: That is certainly correct, in terms of the SPO. I'm saying that. I mean, I heard that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the same paragraph that you discuss the 100 Seselj's men, you also describe "50 armed volunteers"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, these volunteers were -- I mean, how shall I put this? They were people who were neither here nor there. I mean volunteers, volunteers, but no one knew who they were and what they were, because really --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For the 50 we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Fifty, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also say that they were never issued any military cards and they were never registered. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to say -- well, we're talking about these 50. These are volunteers who quite simply came from other fronts to this Herzegovina front. They did not have any military IDs, and they could not get any, because all of us had old military IDs from the JNA. I mean, I served --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How do you know they were never issued these military cards or registered? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV DABIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that. You hear about everything. Don't you understand that? It's not really a big place out there. For example, when you come from the front-line to barracks to take a bath, you hear people talking. You hear about everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: May I inquire how much time I have left, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, well, some five minutes ago the Registrar told me that you'd used 45 minutes. And you had an hour and a half, so you have some 40 minutes left, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could you please suggest to Ms. Biersay, because I did not have occasion to see this footage, could she use that here tonight so that I can prepare, if necessary, for tomorrow? If she shows it tomorrow, then it's no use to me. If she shows it today, then I can prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the video footage; would you like us to see this now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will see how things progress. I would like to get to the two clips, certainly not all 40 minutes of it, but the two clips that we selected and are in your binder as 65 ter numbers 7514A and B. What we could do is to make the tape available. We could burn it onto a DVD if we don't get to it, and Mr. Seselj is more than welcome to use the evening to view it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you see the problem, Ms. Biersay, is that -- one moment, Mr. Seselj. I'm trying to find a solution, a practical solution to a substantial problem. Ms. Biersay, the accused has just discovered that there's this video footage. He hasn't seen the video, and he would like to think about it until tomorrow. And if he could see it now, he would have some time to have a bit of a think about it and he would be better positioned to cross-examine the witness tomorrow. This is your evidence. You decide as to how you want to use it. If you decide not to use it, you would have taken the Trial Chamber's time about it, because I've been looking at it since this morning and I've been working non-stop since 9.00 this morning in this very courtroom. So I took time to look at the video, and now you may not want to use it. That would be an utter waste, indeed. So do you want to use it or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, I didn't suggest that we wouldn't use it. I am looking at the time, and I will use it -- I'm trying to use it in the most efficient way. If I have time left over and I haven't gotten to it today, I'd like to do it tomorrow. And for the record, if the Court remembers that -- the vast disclosure we made of all the videos to Mr. Seselj, and this is one of the videos. Mr. Seselj actually already has it in DVD form. So we're certainly not going to play all 40 minutes this evening.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I informed you that I received that yesterday and that I had no place to watch it. I was fair enough to agree to use 65 ter for that. I did not bring it into question. But it would only be fair if I saw it today so if I have anything to object to, I can prepare for tomorrow, not for me to see it only tomorrow and then immediately get into a discussion of footage that I hadn't seen before that. And I have no place to see it. I do not have the right kind of thing to watch it on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... this matter, because we could decide that it should be viewed straightaway. So I'm going to ask my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, after deliberation the Trial Chamber has decided to view the video footage now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Am I to understand that this will not count in the Prosecution's time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while we're queuing the two videos, and I believe that we have offered to give the 65 ter number: Mr. Seselj has the transcripts of these video-clips, and we transmitted all the materials to him on Friday. While we're waiting for it, this is -- again, the clips are 65 ter number 7514, and the description of it is: Yutel coverage of the situation in Nevesinje, including the men at check-points around Nevesinje. And it has been dated as being sometime in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I would go when I have seen the footage, even if I should stay until midnight. I'll stay until midnight, but I want to see this footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Our case manager is working on resolving the problem, so if the Court would prefer that we take a five-minute break so that we can try to perhaps reload it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall be waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'll try to play it from another media. While that's being done, Your Honours, I believe that a request was made with respect to Mr. Theunens' report, and I can -- I now advise the Court that his report, which is Exhibit P258, in part 2, pages 141 to 149, it shows that it's the -- on page 147, that the 4th Military District covered Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, this has to do with Herzegovina, whereas Ms. Biersay is now talking about Eastern Bosnia. Military districts existed just before the war -- or, rather, before the war, whereas just before the war the entire territory of Yugoslavia was subdivided into three military districts. Before that, there were army districts. The 6th Army District was in Sarajevo. Herzegovina has nothing to do with what Ms. Biersay has been saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a look at page 147 of the Theunens report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So 147 as well as 141 to 149 covers the issue of the 2nd Military District that was in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay, I think we'll try.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That was clip A. And now clip B, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have now seen these two clips. This time will not be counted against you, Ms. Biersay. You'll have 40 minutes tomorrow, and after that Mr. Seselj will have an hour and a half. I hope we'll be able to finish without any further problem. Witness, I remind you that you're not supposed to speak or have contact with anybody at all. Please be here tomorrow in the afternoon. We shall begin at 2.15, and I'm sure that Ms. Biersay will have questions for you based on the two video-clips we've just viewed. I wish you all a good evening.
